text.assumption: Assumes {sip_plan_rate} a year throughout, and {price_rise_rate} inflation. Returns are never guaranteed.

voice.s1: Suppose you have a fixed amount of money, and {sip_plan_years} years ahead of you. Do you feed it into the market slowly, month after month, or put all of it in on day one and then leave it completely alone? Most people assume the difference between those two is small. It is not. The gap is far bigger than almost anyone guesses, and by the end of this you will know exactly why, and which one actually applies to your situation.
voice.s2: Before we go anywhere near the answer, let us make this a genuinely fair fight. The same total amount of money goes in, either way. Not a rupee more on one side than the other. The same assumed rate of return, year after year, applied to both. The same stretch of time, {sip_plan_years} years, from the first day to the last. Everything that could quietly tilt the result is held still. The only thing we change is the timing. One route drips the money in month by month. The other hands all of it over at the very start and never touches it again. That single difference is the whole experiment.
voice.s3: Route one is the one you almost certainly already know, because it is how a salary works. A fixed amount, {sip_plan_amount}, leaves your account every month, for {sip_plan_years} years, without fail. You never try to guess the right moment. You never skip a month because the news looks frightening. At the end of it, your own contributions come to {sip_plan_invested}, and growth has quietly added {sip_plan_gains} on top. That is the number most people have in their heads when they think about long term investing.
voice.s4: Route two uses exactly the same money, {lump_plan_amount}, but all of it goes in on the very first day. After that you do nothing at all for {lump_plan_years} years. No monthly transfer, no decisions, no checking. The same amount leaves your pocket as in route one. What comes back is a very different number, and this is the part that surprises people the first time they run it properly.
voice.s5: Here they are side by side, and the difference is hard to argue with. Identical money going in. Identical returns along the way. Identical number of years. The monthly route grows your money {sip_plan_ratio}. The lump sum route grows it {lump_plan_ratio}. Same effort, same risk, same market, and yet one of them ends up far ahead of the other. If you have ever been told that a monthly plan beats a lump sum on pure returns, this is the comparison that was never actually run.
voice.s6: Now watch the same story as a picture, because the shape of it explains everything. In the first few years the two lines sit close together and it all looks fairly boring. Then the lump sum line starts to pull away. And the further right you go, the faster that gap widens, until by the end the two are nowhere near each other. That is not because one investment is cleverer than the other. It is because one of them has been compounding on the full amount since day one, while the other is still being fed in slowly, a little at a time, with each new instalment arriving too late to catch up.
voice.s7: The reason is simple once you see it, and it has nothing to do with picking better funds. In the lump sum route, every single rupee gets the complete {lump_plan_years} years to compound. Nothing is sitting in your bank account waiting its turn. In a monthly plan, the money arrives in pieces. Your very first instalment does get the full run. Your second gets a month less. And your final instalment, paid in the last month, grows for about thirty days before you stop. Average all of that out and half your money has had only half the time.
voice.s8: So if the maths is this clear, why does almost everybody use a monthly plan anyway? Because the comparison quietly assumes something most of us simply do not have: a large pile of money sitting idle today, doing nothing. A monthly plan lets you invest money you have not even earned yet. It also removes the single hardest decision in investing, which is choosing the moment to begin. And when prices fall, which they will, the same fixed amount quietly buys you more units than it did last month. None of that shows up in the final number, but all of it matters.
voice.s9: So here is the practical version, the part you can actually act on this week. If a bonus, a maturity, or any windfall lands in your hands, put it to work sooner rather than carefully slicing it into small monthly pieces, because slicing it is just recreating the slower route on purpose. Keep the monthly plan running underneath all of it, through good months and bad. And every single time your salary goes up, raise that monthly amount before you get used to the extra money.
voice.s10: Three things worth carrying away from all of this. First, if the money is already in your hands today, investing it at once beats trickling it in, and the gap is large. Second, in real life the money arrives monthly, which is exactly why the monthly plan is the honest answer for most people. And third, waiting is the one choice that loses either way, because prices keep climbing while you make up your mind. {price_rise_amount} left alone today is worth about {price_rise_final} in {price_rise_years} years.
voice.s11: The best route is not the cleverest one on a spreadsheet. It is the one you can actually keep up for {sip_plan_years} years without talking yourself out of it halfway through. If this was useful, subscribe, and tell me in the comments which route you are on right now.
